before: Hospitalization and In-Hospital Mortality Trends for Primary Malignant Brain Tumors in Ecuador: A 10-Year Population Study
after: Hospitalizations and In Hospital Deaths Associated With Malignant Brain Neoplasms in Ecuador From 2015 to 2024

before: Primary malignant brain tumors pose a major public health challenge in low- and middle-income countries, yet long-term nationwide hospital discharge records data from the Andean region remain scarce. This study evaluates 10-year nationwide trends, anatomical distributions, and determinants of hospitalization and in-hospital mortality in Ecuador (2015–2024). Nationwide retrospective analysis of hospital discharge records registries standardized to the 2022 Ecuadorian Census. Age-adjusted hospitalization (AAHR) and in-hospital mortality rates (AAIMR) per 100,000 population were calculated. Adjusted odds ratios () and relative risk ratios () were estimated using multivariate logistic models. The overall 10-year mean AAHR was 4.859 per 100,000 population, and the AAIMR stood at 0.461 per 100,000. Furthermore, the overall in-hospital case-fatality proportion was 9.61%.
after: This study describes nationwide hospitalizations, anatomical coding and in-hospital deaths associated with malignant brain neoplasm discharge diagnoses in Ecuador during 2015–2024. We analyzed annual INEC discharge records with primary diagnosis C71.0–C71.9. Resident-population rates were directly standardized to the observed 2022 Ecuadorian census age distribution using annual population estimates. Binary logistic models estimated adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for death, coding detail and conditional anatomical group. The reconstruction included 10,972 admissions and 963 deaths; admission fatality was 8.78% (95% CI 8.26–9.32). Resident rates excluded three foreign-resident live discharges. The mean annual age-adjusted hospitalization rate (AAHR) was 6.611 per 100,000 residents (95% CI 6.487–6.737), and the corresponding in-hospital death rate (AAIMR) was 0.598 (0.561–0.638).

A drop in total AAHR occurred during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 (5.322 per 100,000). The recorded frequency of unspecified anatomical coding decreased by 2024, as the unspecified tumor AAHR dropped to 0.000 per 100,000. Multivariate regression revealed that older age ( for 80 years, ) and extended hospital stays (30 days: ) were associated with lower odds of in-hospital death, longer hospital stays were inversely associated with in-hospital mortality; however, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because length of stay is partly determined by survival time. Hospitalization and mortality burdens remained stable, driven by acute early-stay mortality and public sector concentration. The decrease in unspecified coding over time provides a critical baseline to guide regional neuro-oncological policy and resource distribution.
after: Older age was associated with higher adjusted death odds: ages ≥80 versus 0–17 had an aOR of 2.631 (95% CI 1.864–3.715). Unspecified C71.9 coding accounted for 4,668 admissions (42.54%), including 379 in 2024. Among 6,192 records assigned to either anatomical group, ages 0–17 versus 18–44 had an aOR of 1.141 (0.985–1.320) for infratentorial/midline versus supratentorial coding; estimates varied by period. These results describe hospital service events and deaths during admission. Unspecified coding, selected inpatient populations and unresolved repeat-admission dependence limit interpretation.

before: Malignant brain tumors comprise a heterogeneous group of central nervous system neoplasms characterized by infiltrative growth, a high burden of morbidity, and elevated mortality. Although their incidence is lower than that of many other cancer types, they represent a major cause of disability and death because of their anatomical location, biological behavior, and limited response to available therapeutic interventions  . These neoplasms include both primary tumors and metastatic lesions, with high-grade gliomas being the most common primary malignant brain tumors. Early diagnosis and advances in histopathological and molecular characterization have improved tumor classification and clinical management; however, survival remains limited in most hospitalizations .
after: Malignant brain tumors comprise a heterogeneous group of central nervous system neoplasms. Histological and molecular characterization informs their classification and clinical interpretation. Administrative discharge codes describe anatomical sites but do not provide the integrated histological and molecular classification used in neuro-oncology [19]. This analysis concerns diagnoses coded C71.0–C71.9; neither histological confirmation nor primary tumor origin can be established from a primary discharge diagnosis alone [2].

before: These neoplasms include both primary tumors and metastatic lesions, with high-grade gliomas being the most common primary malignant brain tumors. Early diagnosis and advances in histopathological and molecular characterization have improved tumor classification and clinical management; however, survival remains limited in most hospitalizations , in this context, epidemiological and clinical research is essential to improve the understanding of their biological behavior and to guide strategies for prevention, diagnosis, and treatment.

Globally, malignant brain tumors represent a relatively uncommon but highly lethal group of cancers, imposing a disproportionate burden on health systems due to their poor prognosis and substantial neurological sequelae. According to GLOBOCAN 2022, approximately 321,700 new hospitalizations and 248,500 deaths from brain and central nervous system cancers were estimated worldwide, highlighting their high case-fatality despite their comparatively low incidence . The geographic distribution of malignant brain tumors exhibits substantial regional variation, influenced by differences in population structure, diagnostic capacity, cancer registration systems, environmental exposures, and access to specialized neuro-oncology care. These disparities highlight the importance of strengthening epidemiological surveillance and improving equitable access to timely diagnosis and treatment .
after: Hospital-discharge records provide a complementary description of inpatient care and outcomes during admission. They do not identify incident cancers, unique patients or deaths outside the included hospital stays. Distinguishing these endpoints is essential when interpreting hospitalization rates alongside cancer incidence and mortality estimates [1,8].

before: In Latin America and the Caribbean, malignant brain tumors represent a significant public health challenge because of their high lethality and unequal access to specialized diagnostic and treatment services. According to GLOBOCAN 2022, approximately 27,000 new hospitalizations and more than 22,500 deaths from brain and central nervous system cancers were estimated across the region . Incidence and mortality vary considerably among countries, reflecting differences in population-based cancer registration, diagnostic capacity, and access to specialized oncology care. These disparities highlight the need to strengthen epidemiological surveillance and regional cancer control strategies .
after: In Latin America, regional research has described brain and central nervous system cancer incidence using cancer registries and mortality using WHO data, with world-standardized rates [20]. Those endpoints and standards differ from the admission-based measures examined here; direct numerical comparison requires matched definitions and populations.

before: In Ecuador, malignant brain tumors are relatively uncommon neoplasms but remain associated with substantial mortality and disability because of their aggressive clinical behavior. According to GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, approximately 561 new hospitalizations of brain and central nervous system cancers and 463 related deaths were recorded in Ecuador . Despite their lower incidence compared with other malignancies, diagnosis frequently occurs at advanced stages, and access to specialized neuro-oncology services remains uneven across the country. These challenges highlight the need to strengthen epidemiological surveillance and improve timely diagnosis and treatment strategies .
after: According to the archived GLOBOCAN 2024 estimates, version 1.0, 561 new brain and central nervous system cancer cases and 463 related deaths were estimated in Ecuador, both sexes and all ages [18]. These are modeled cancer estimates, not observed hospital admissions. Hospital-discharge analysis can complement this context by describing recorded inpatient activity and deaths during admission.

before: Accordingly, this study aimed to characterize the hospitalization burden of malignant brain tumors in Ecuador from 2015 to 2024 by examining age-adjusted hospitalization, in-hospital mortality rates, geographic distribution, anatomical patterns, sociodemographic and institutional factors associated with hospital outcomes.
after: Accordingly, this study aimed to characterize the hospitalization burden associated with malignant brain neoplasm discharge codes in Ecuador from 2015 to 2024 by examining age-adjusted hospitalization and in-hospital death rates, geographic distribution, anatomical coding, and sociodemographic and institutional associations with hospital outcomes. Coding detail and conditional anatomical group were analyzed as separate exploratory questions.

before: We performed a retrospective observational study based on hospital discharge records collected by INEC between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2024. The INEC database aggregates comprehensive inpatient admissions across public, private, and social security healthcare institutions spanning all 24 provinces of Ecuador. This manuscript was prepared following the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines to ensure transparent and reproducible methodology.
after:
We performed a retrospective repeated cross-sectional analysis of discharge records in Ecuador's annual INEC Registro Estadístico de Camas y Egresos Hospitalarios releases for 2015–2024. The source is a national administrative operation, rather than a population cancer registry. Records represent discharges in the relevant annual release, including stays beginning before that year. National scope does not establish complete capture of every cancer admission or institution. We accessed the annual released SPSS files and available dictionaries, not clinical records or a restricted patient-identification database. [1, 8]

Annual releases and available dictionaries were acquired on 23 October 2026; additional early-year syntax materials were inspected during the audit. Source URLs, acquisition timestamps, archive members, versions where identifiable and SHA-256 fingerprints are provided in the supplementary source manifests. Population workbooks were acquired separately on 6 November 2026. These national inputs were used to reconstruct the analysis independently of the previously supplied SAV, SPV and two XLSX files, which constitute the complete original analysis package. The reconstructed and historical cohorts are not interchangeable. [1, 3, 4]

after: Infratentorial and midline: C71.5 (brain ventricles), C71.6 (cerebellum), and C71.7 (brainstem). This is an operational grouping: C71.5 is not universally infratentorial. A sensitivity analysis excluded C71.5 [2].

before: Overlapping Lesions: C71.8 (overlapping malignant lesions of the brain).
after: Overlapping lesions: C71.8. These records were retained descriptively and in the coding-detail panel, without assignment to a single anatomical compartment [2].

before: Unspecified / Other: C71.9 (malignant neoplasm of the brain, unspecified).
after: Unspecified: C71.9 (malignant neoplasm of the brain, unspecified). This is a documentation category, not a biological anatomical site [2].

before: The primary dependent variable for the binary outcomes was patient survival at discharge, recorded as a binary variable (0 = Alive, 1 = Deceased). For the multinomial frameworks, the dependent outcome was the anatomical tumor category.
after: The primary outcome was death during the recorded admission, explicitly coded as death=1 for source discharge codes 2/3 and live discharge=0 for source code 1. Observation ended at discharge; there was no postdischarge survival follow-up. Separate binary outcomes represented non-C71.9 coding versus C71.9 and infratentorial/midline versus supratentorial coding in the eligible subset.

before: Categorical variables were summarized using absolute frequencies () and proportions (). Group differences across survival status (Dead vs. Alive) and anatomical tumor groups were evaluated using Pearson’s chi-square () test or Fisher’s exact test when expected cell counts were below 5 in more than 20% of the cross-tabulation cells.
after: Categorical variables were summarized using counts and column percentages; within-category fatality used deaths divided by admissions in that category. One exploratory omnibus comparison was performed per characteristic. Pearson chi-square without continuity correction was used when every active observed and expected cell was at least five. Sparse 2×2 tables used two-sided Fisher exact; other sparse tables used fixed-margin Monte Carlo Pearson tests with 99,999 draws and deterministic seeds. The simulated p-value was (exceedances+1)/(draws+1), including ties. No multiplicity adjustment or significance highlighting was used [17].

before: Binary Logistic Regression: Evaluated independent risk factors for in-hospital mortality. Adjusted Odds Ratios (aOR) and 95% Confidence Intervals (95% CI) were calculated, adjusting for age group, sex, ethnicity, area of residence, health sector, ICD-10 anatomical group, length of stay, and year of discharge.
after: We estimated maximum-likelihood binary logistic models for exploratory admission-level associations, not causal effects or validated prediction. The death model included categorical age, sex, all source ethnicity categories, binary sector, recorded anatomical group and discharge year, with 27 parameters including the intercept. References were ages 0–17, male, Mestizo (source code 6), private sector, supratentorial group and 2015. It included 10,972 admissions and 963 deaths, with no primary complete-case exclusions. before: Multinomial Logistic Regression: Evaluated sociodemographic and institutional predictors of specific anatomical locations (Infratentorial/Midline, Overlapping Lesions, and Supratentorial). The "Unspecified / Other" group served as the baseline reference category due to its unordered categorical nature. Results are presented as Adjusted Relative Risk Ratios (aRRR) with 95% CIs.
after: Two separate primary models addressed recorded coding and anatomy. The coding model used non-C71.9 diagnoses (C71.0–C71.8) as event 1 and C71.9 as reference 0, including 10,972 records and 6,304 events. C71.8 was included without implying a single recorded site. The conditional-site model used infratentorial/midline C71.5–C71.7 as event 1 and supratentorial C71.0–C71.4 as reference 0; it included 6,192 records and 1,523 events after excluding 112 C71.8 and 4,668 C71.9 records. Both models adjusted for age group, sex, binary sector and categorical year, with 16 parameters including the intercept and references ages 18–44, male, private sector and 2015. Ethnicity was descriptive and used in separate extended sensitivity models, not primary anatomy/coding adjustment.

before: Covariate selection was driven by data availability in the INEC database and informed by established literature on social determinants in neuro-oncology. All statistical tests were two-tailed, with significance defined at . Data processing and modeling were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics (Version 25.0, Armonk, NY, USA).
after: Covariates provided limited descriptive adjustment, not complete confounding control. No significance-based selection or interaction search was performed. Models were checked for full rank, separation, convergence, finite estimates, score residuals and positive information eigenvalues. All eight death-model and 15 coding/site fits passed these checks. Primary intervals and p-values were Wald-based; sparse contrasts were supplemented with profile-likelihood intervals. The revised analysis used Python 3.14.7, pandas 3.1.0, SciPy 1.18.1 and statsmodels 0.15.0. The historical SPSS output was audited but was not reused as a validated estimate [13–16].

before: This study analyzed publicly available, secondary administrative registries managed by the National Institute of Statistics and Censuses (INEC) of Ecuador. The dataset is fully anonymized and stripped of all personal identifiers prior to release. Consequently, the study presented no potential risk to participants, and informed consent was not required in accordance with international ethical standards for secondary data research and national regulations overseen by the Human Research Ethics Committee (CEISH-INSPI).
after: This study analyzed publicly released secondary hospital-discharge records from INEC. No clinical records or restricted patient-identification database were accessed.

before: Between 2015 and 2024, a total of 8,249 hospital admissions with a primary diagnosis of malignant brain tumor were recorded in Ecuador, of which 793 resulted in in-hospital death, corresponding to an overall in-hospital case-fatality proportion of 9.61% (). Bivariate analysis revealed significant disparities in mortality across age groups (), where older adults aged 45–64 years concentrated the highest proportion of fatal hospitalizations (31.0%), whereas younger cohorts (0–44 years) accounted for over half of all admissions resulting in live discharge (56.5%). Geographic and institutional barriers significantly influenced outcomes; rural residents ( vs. , ) and patients treated in public sector facilities ( vs. , ) experienced higher proportions of in-hospital deaths compared to their urban and private-sector counterparts. Furthermore, prolonged hospitalization was strongly associated with mortality (), with extended stays of 30 days being more than twice as frequent among admissions resulting in in-hospital death compared to survivors ( vs. ). Neither sex () nor ICD-10 anatomical tumor location () demonstrated statistically significant differences in crude in-hospital survival (Table 1).
after: Between 2015 and 2024, the reconstructed cohort included 10,972 hospital admissions with a primary C71 diagnosis, of which 963 ended in death and 10,009 in live discharge. Overall admission fatality was 8.78% (95% CI 8.26–9.32). Ages 45–64 accounted for 294 deaths (30.53% of deaths); ages 0–44 accounted for 5,694 live discharges (56.89% of live discharges). Crude fatality was 9.36% in the public sector and 7.89% in the private sector. These descriptive comparisons do not establish institutional performance or access barriers. Counts, explicit denominators and exploratory comparisons are shown in Table 1.

after: Recorded anatomical groups comprised 4,669 supratentorial, 1,523 infratentorial/midline, 112 overlapping and 4,668 unspecified admissions. Table 2 presents the distributions by age, sex, ethnicity, sector, recorded stay, year and verified residence period. These are recorded code groups; differences do not establish biological site propensity or diagnostic accuracy.

before: Between 2015 and 2024, the overall 10-year mean Age-Adjusted Hospitalization Rate (AAHR) for primary malignant brain tumors in Ecuador was 4.859 per 100,000 population. Excluding years with unusually low recorded hospitalization counts in 2017 (0.185 per 100,000) and 2023 (0.485 per 100,000), admission rates remained stable between 5.322 and 6.393 per 100,000 inhabitants, reaching a peak in 2019 (6.393 per 100,000) and dropping in 2020 (5.322 per 100,000) coinciding with the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. Unspecified neoplasms recorded the highest 10-year mean AAHR (2.086 per 100,000), followed closely by supratentorial lesions (1.996 per 100,000). Notably, the recorded frequency of unspecified anatomical coding decreased by 2024, as the unspecified rate dropped to 0.000 per 100,000 while supratentorial admissions reached a study period high of 2.747 per 100,000.
after: Between 2015 and 2024, the mean annual AAHR was 6.611 per 100,000 residents (95% CI 6.487–6.737). All ten years were retained. The highest total rate occurred in 2017 (7.583), and the lowest in 2020 (5.540). The 2024 total was 5.784, including an unspecified rate of 2.152 from 379 admissions. Supratentorial hospitalization rates peaked in 2019 (3.470), not 2024. These changes describe timing, without a formal trend or causal pandemic analysis.

before: The 10-year mean Age-Adjusted In-Hospital Mortality Rate (AAIMR) stood at 0.461 per 100,000 population, remaining remarkably stable excluding 2017 and 2023 with peak rates observed in 2015 and 2018 (0.561 per 100,000). By anatomical localization, unspecified tumors (0.220 per 100,000) and supratentorial lesions (0.182 per 100,000) accounted for over 87% of the total standardized mortality burden nationwide, whereas infratentorial/midline lesions (0.062 per 100,000) and overlapping tumors (0.004 per 100,000) contributed minimally to overall population-level mortality (Table 3).
after: The mean annual AAIMR was 0.598 per 100,000 residents (95% CI 0.561–0.638), with its highest value in 2017 (0.758) and lowest in 2020 (0.454). Unspecified and supratentorial components together accounted for 86.157% of the mean standardized in-hospital death rate. This is a standardized rate contribution, not the raw proportion of deaths. Table 3 provides the annual estimates and intervals.

before: Age-adjusted hospitalization and in-hospital mortality rates for malignant brain tumors showed substantial temporal variation in Ecuador between 2015 and 2024. Hospitalization rates remained relatively stable at approximately 5–6 hospitalizations per 100,000 population during most years, reaching their highest value in 2019 (6.393 per 100,000), while pronounced reductions were observed in 2017 (0.185) and 2023 (0.485). Supratentorial (hemispheric) and unspecified/other tumors accounted for the largest components of the hospitalization rates across most of the study period. Age-adjusted in-hospital mortality rates were considerably lower, generally ranging from 0.428 to 0.561 per 100,000 in years other than 2017, with the lowest value recorded in 2017 (0.060). Overall, the temporal patterns indicate fluctuations in both hospitalization and mortality rates, with particularly atypical values in 2017 and 2023 that warrant cautious interpretation.
after: Age-adjusted hospitalization and in-hospital death rates varied over the study period (Figure 1). Supratentorial and unspecified codes contributed the largest hospitalization-rate components. The severe 2017 and 2023 deficits in the historical extract were not reproduced by the official-source reconstruction; these years were retained without labeling them registration failures.

before: After controlling for sociodemographic, spatial, and clinical covariates, multivariate binary logistic regression revealed that age group and length of hospital stay were the primary independent predictors of in-hospital survival. Compared to admissions aged 0–17 years, older age cohorts demonstrated significantly lower adjusted odds of in-hospital death, ranging from  (, ) in individuals aged 45–64 years to  (, ) in those aged 80 years. Length of hospital stay was significantly associated with in-hospital mortality. Compared with admissions lasting 1–3 days, stays of 15–30 days (aOR = 0.710, 95% CI: 0.556–0.907; p = 0.006) and ≥30 days (aOR = 0.288, 95% CI: 0.222–0.372; p < 0.001) were associated with lower adjusted odds of in-hospital death. These associations should not be interpreted as evidence of a protective effect of prolonged hospitalization, because length of stay is partly determined by survival time during hospitalization. (Table 4).
after: After adjustment for recorded covariates, older age groups had higher odds of death during admission than ages 0–17: aOR 1.593 (95% CI 1.312–1.934) for ages 45–64, 2.153 (1.742–2.661) for 65–79, and 2.631 (1.864–3.715) for ≥80. The public/private aOR was 1.201 (1.035–1.394), while 2023 versus 2015 was 1.034 (0.768–1.391). These are conditional associations, not causal effects or survival probabilities (Table 4). Final stay was excluded from the primary model.

before: Multinomial logistic regression identified age, ethnicity, area of residence, health sector, and length of stay as independent predictors of anatomical tumor site relative to unspecified neoplasms. Pediatric age (0–17 years) significantly increased the relative risk of infratentorial and midline tumor diagnoses (, , ). Mestizo ethnicity was associated with higher relative risk for both supratentorial (, ) and infratentorial (, ) diagnoses. Institutional determinants were notable: private healthcare facilities recorded significantly lower relative odds for supratentorial (, ) and overlapping lesions (, ) compared to public centers. Rural residence was associated with reduced relative odds of supratentorial tumors (, ). Neither sex nor patient age showed significant associations with supratentorial localization relative to unspecified lesions (Table 5).
after: The coding-detail model included 10,972 admissions, with 6,304 non-C71.9 events. The conditional anatomical model included 6,192 admissions, with 1,523 infratentorial/midline events, after excluding 112 overlapping and 4,668 unspecified records. In the latter model, ages 0–17 versus 18–44 had an aOR of 1.141 (95% CI 0.985–1.320). Table 5 presents the two separate binary panels, with age 18–44, male, private sector and 2015 as references. These aORs do not reproduce the former multinomial estimand.

before: The spatial distribution of malignant brain tumors showed marked heterogeneity across Ecuadorian provinces during 2015–2024. Pichincha and Guayas consistently concentrated the highest numbers of hospitalizations, reaching their maximum values in 2019 (427 hospitalizations) and 2016 (449 hospitalizations), respectively. Azuay represented another relevant concentration, particularly between 2018 and 2022, whereas Manabí and Loja showed intermediate numbers and variations throughout the study period. In contrast, several Amazonian provinces and Galápagos reported considerably fewer hospitalizations. An exceptional reduction in recorded hospitalizations was observed in 2017 and 2023 across nearly the entire country, followed by an increase in subsequent years; this pattern should be interpreted with caution, as it may reflect changes in data recording or availability rather than a true decline in disease occurrence. Overall, the maps reveal a persistent concentration of hospitalizations mainly in Pichincha, Guayas, and, to a lesser extent, Azuay.
after: Figure 2 displays admission counts for all 24 provinces of residence and ten discharge years, comprising 10,969 resident records. Three foreign-resident live discharges were excluded; no unknown residence-province codes occurred. The annual cartographic presentation is supplied in Figure S1; Figure S2 separately assigns all 10,972 records to treating-facility province. These counts describe recorded service events, not provincial cancer incidence, population risk, referral severity or access. The early rural/urban label uncertainty does not determine province assignment.

before: This study provides the first decade-long (2015–2024) nationwide evaluation of age-adjusted hospitalization (AAHR: 4.859 per 100,000) and in-hospital mortality rates (AAIMR: 0.461 per 100,000) for primary malignant brain tumors in Ecuador . The primary novelty lies in uncovering critical demographic and administrative transitions: pediatric hospitalizations (17 years) concentrated nearly half of all infratentorial/midline neoplasms (, ), whereas adult cohorts predominated in supratentorial sites . Furthermore, longitudinal tracking revealed a pronounced decrease in unspecified tumor coding () alongside a historical peak in supratentorial diagnoses () by 2024 . Extended hospital stays (≥30 days) were associated with lower adjusted odds of in-hospital death (aOR = 0.288). However, this finding should be interpreted cautiously because length of stay is inherently conditioned by survival during hospitalization; patients must survive long enough to enter the prolonged-stay category. Therefore, this association should not be interpreted as evidence that prolonged hospitalization confers a protective effect against in-hospital mortality.
after: This study provides a nationwide evaluation of recorded C71-coded hospitalizations and in-hospital deaths during 2015–2024. The mean annual standardized hospitalization rate was 6.611 per 100,000 residents and the corresponding in-hospital death rate was 0.598. Unspecified coding remained frequent, including 379 admissions in 2024. These findings describe inpatient activity and documentation, without establishing cancer incidence, overall cancer mortality or improved diagnostic accuracy.

before: Our multivariate model revealed a counterintuitive inverse association between advanced age and in-hospital mortality, with patients aged  years demonstrating significantly lower adjusted odds of death () compared to pediatric admissions. This finding must be interpreted cautiously and should not be construed as a protective effect of advanced age. Rather, it likely reflects strong hospital selection bias and 'case mix' differences. In low-and middle-income settings, elderly patients with terminal neuro-oncological conditions or severe comorbidities may experience out-of-hospital mortality, receive palliative care at home, or be deemed ineligible for aggressive inpatient surgical interventions. Consequently, the  years cohort admitted to tertiary hospitals may represent a highly selected subgroup of patients with better performance status or more favorable baseline characteristics, whereas the pediatric reference group often undergoes intensive, high-risk surgical procedures that carry inherent immediate mortality risks.
after: Our multivariable model identified higher adjusted death odds in older age groups relative to pediatric admissions. This association remains conditional on admission and the recorded adjustment set. Histology, grade, comorbidity, treatment, referral severity and palliative intent were unavailable; selection into inpatient care and unmeasured case mix may affect these associations. The estimates do not establish a causal age effect or validate a prediction model.

before: While male predominance was consistently observed across all anatomical sites ( to ), sex was not an independent predictor of mortality or tumor localization . During the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic (2020), total hospitalization rates dropped sharply to  per 100,000 (down from  in 2019), reflecting severe health system strain, deferred elective surgical admissions, and delayed neuroimaging access across Ecuador . However, in-hospital mortality remained relatively stable (), suggesting that emergency care for critically ill neuro-oncological admissions was prioritized . Moreover, the extreme rate reductions in 2017 (0.185) and 2023 (0.485) could reflect completeness issues of the registry or data capture disruptions rather than true epidemiological shifts in population burden.
after: During the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, 2020, total hospitalization and in-hospital death rates were the lowest in the observed series. This timing does not establish a pandemic effect. The data cannot distinguish changes in presentation, admission practice, care availability or recording, and do not demonstrate emergency prioritization. The reconstructed 2017 and 2023 counts do not support the historical extract-based claims of national registry disruptions.

before: Ecuador’s overall hospitalization metrics align closely with rates reported across Latin America and other developing regions (e.g., Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, Peru, India, and China), where rates generally range between 3.5 and 6.0 per 100,000 population . These figures contrast sharply with high-income settings, such as North America and Western Europe, which consistently document higher rates (7.0 to 11.5 per 100,000) due to ubiquitous 3T MRI accessibility, integrated electronic registries, and higher diagnostic rates in geriatric populations  . In low-to-middle-income countries (LMICs), lower observed rates are frequently influenced by underdiagnosis, diagnostic infrastructure gaps in rural zones, and lower inpatient admission rates among elderly terminal patients . The heavy reliance on public facilities for complex hospitalizations in Ecuador ( for supratentorial lesions) mirrors broader structural patterns across Latin American public health systems.
after: International comparison requires compatible endpoints, diagnosis definitions and standard populations. Cancer-incidence and population-mortality estimates are not direct benchmarks for hospitalization rates [18,20]. Similarly, the observed public/private association cannot establish hospital quality, access barriers or tertiary case complexity, because clinical severity and referral pathways were not measured adequately.

before: This investigation has several limitations inherent to secondary administrative health datasets . Because the INEC administrative database does not allow longitudinal identification of unique individuals, the unit of analysis was the hospitalization rather than the patient; therefore, repeated admissions of the same individual may be represented as separate records. Hospital discharge registries (INEC) are susceptible to misclassification, coding heterogeneity across clinical centers, and single-year capture anomalies (2017 and 2023) . Furthermore, ICD-10 coding lacks integrated WHO molecular and histopathological granularity (e.g., IDH mutation status, MGMT methylation, or 1p/19q codeletion) . Finally, the dataset strictly captures in-hospital deaths, thereby excluding out-of-hospital or home-based palliative mortality.
after: This investigation has several limitations inherent to secondary administrative health datasets. Because the INEC records do not allow longitudinal identification of unique individuals, the unit of analysis was the hospitalization rather than the patient; repeated admissions may appear as separate records. Patient and facility clustering could not be resolved with validated identifiers, so reported intervals condition on independent records and may understate uncertainty. Discharge diagnoses were not clinically validated and may be misclassified. ICD-10 codes do not provide integrated WHO histological/molecular classification [19]. The dataset captures deaths during admission, excluding postdischarge and out-of-hospital deaths.

By documenting the reduction of unspecified anatomical coding alongside persistent public-private healthcare access disparities, these findings establish a crucial epidemiological baseline to inform future neuro-oncological health policies . Ultimately, these epidemiological insights provide actionable data for resource allocation, neuro-oncological referral pathways, and specialized surgical infrastructure development across the Andean region .

The coding-detail and conditional-site models answer distinct questions; exclusion of unspecified and overlapping codes from the site model does not correct nonrandom selection. These results provide a descriptive basis for future clinical validation and linkage research rather than demonstrated effects of resource allocation or care policies.

before: This 10-year nationwide study provides the first comprehensive population-based baseline of age-adjusted hospitalization and in-hospital mortality rates for primary malignant brain tumors in Ecuador. Over the past decade, overall hospitalization and mortality burden remained relatively stable during most of the study period, with significant demographic, institutional, and clinical disparities shaping patient outcomes. Pediatric hospitalizations concentrated a disproportionate burden of infratentorial and midline neoplasms, whereas supratentorial tumors predominated in adults and older cohorts. Multivariate modeling identified significant associations between age group, length of hospital stays, and in-hospital mortality. The inverse association observed for prolonged hospital stays should be interpreted cautiously because length of stay is conditioned by survival during hospitalization and may therefore be affected by reverse causation and time-related bias.
after: This ten-year nationwide analysis describes C71-coded hospital admissions and deaths during admission in Ecuador. Older age was associated with higher adjusted death odds, while frequent unspecified coding and period-sensitive anatomical associations limit interpretation. Final length of stay is outcome-dependent and should not be interpreted as a protective or harmful baseline exposure.

before: Furthermore, institutional analysis highlights significant disparities between public and private healthcare sectors, with public tertiary facilities managing the vast majority of complex supratentorial and overlapping lesions. Notably, temporal trends demonstrate changes in national health registries, characterized by the progressive decrease of unspecified anatomical coding by 2024. These findings underscore the urgent need for targeted public health strategies, equitable distribution of specialized neuro-oncological resources, and streamlined referral networks to mitigate early in-hospital mortality and reduce care barriers across the Andean region.
after: These findings provide a reproducible description of recorded inpatient activity. They do not estimate cancer incidence or overall cancer mortality, validate diagnostic accuracy, or establish public/private differences in care quality. Future work linking clinical information and longitudinal outcomes could address these limitations.
